title: Docker Complete Handbook
summary: A start-to-production tour of Docker. It covers architecture and internals, images and containers, Dockerfile and build optimization, storage, networking, Compose, registries, security, debugging, orchestration, and interview prep.

chapters.title: Docker at a Glance
points: Docker packages an app plus its dependencies into an image that runs the same on a laptop, in CI and in production
Container vs VM: containers share the host kernel and start in milliseconds, while VMs boot a full guest OS
Core nouns: image (read-only template), container (running instance), registry (image store), Dockerfile (build recipe)
Handbook map: architecture, images, Dockerfile, storage, networking, Compose, registries, security, debugging, production
Docker's value: reproducible builds, immutable artifacts, fast startup, dense packing of workloads
Docker is not a security boundary equal to a VM, because all containers share one kernel

chapters.title: Docker Architecture and Internals
points: Client-server model: the docker CLI talks to the dockerd daemon over a REST API on /var/run/docker.sock
dockerd delegates to containerd (lifecycle and image management), which calls runc (the OCI runtime that creates the container)
containerd-shim keeps a container running even if dockerd or containerd restarts
Namespaces isolate what a process sees: pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user, cgroup
cgroups limit and account for resources: CPU, memory, block I/O, PIDs
Union filesystem (overlay2) stacks read-only image layers under one writable container layer
OCI specs standardize the image format and runtime, so images run on Docker, Podman or containerd alike
Docker Desktop on Mac and Windows runs dockerd inside a hidden Linux VM, since containers need a Linux kernel
Example: docker run alpine echo hi triggers CLI → dockerd → containerd → shim → runc → process exits
Mistake: mounting docker.sock into a container hands it root-equivalent control of the host
Interview Point: What does runc do? How do namespaces differ from cgroups? Why does a container die when its PID 1 exits?

chapters.title: Images and Layers
points: An image is an immutable stack of layers plus a JSON config (env, entrypoint, cmd, exposed ports)
Each Dockerfile instruction that changes the filesystem (RUN, COPY, ADD) creates a layer
Layers are content-addressed by SHA256 digest, so identical layers are stored once and shared across images
A tag like nginx:1.27 is a movable pointer, while a digest like nginx@sha256:... is immutable
Copy-on-write: a container changing a lower-layer file copies it into its writable layer first
Deleting a file in a later layer only hides it, and the bytes still ship in the earlier layer
Base images compared: ubuntu (large, familiar), alpine (~5 MB, musl libc), debian-slim, distroless (no shell), scratch (empty)
Example: docker history myapp shows each layer with its size, and docker image inspect shows the config
Mistake: using :latest in production, which makes deployments non-reproducible
Mistake: leaving secrets or build caches in a layer, where they stay recoverable with docker history
Interview Point: How are layers shared between images? Why does deleting a file in a later layer not shrink the image? Tag vs digest?

chapters.title: Containers: Lifecycle and Runtime
points: A container is a running (or stopped) instance of an image with its own writable layer, namespaces and cgroups
States: created, running, paused, stopped (exited), removed
docker run = create + start, and -d detaches, -it attaches an interactive TTY, --rm removes the container on exit
docker stop sends SIGTERM, waits (default 10s), then sends SIGKILL, whereas docker kill sends SIGKILL immediately
The main process is PID 1, which does not get default signal handlers, so apps must handle SIGTERM themselves
Use --init (tini) to reap zombie processes and forward signals properly
Resource limits: --memory 512m, --cpus 1.5, --pids-limit 200, and exceeding memory means an OOM kill (exit 137)
Restart policies: no, on-failure[:N], always, unless-stopped
docker exec runs a new process in a running container, while docker attach connects to the main process's stdio
Example: docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 --restart unless-stopped nginx
Mistake: expecting data in the writable layer to survive docker rm
Interview Point: What does exit code 137 mean? Difference between exec and attach? Why does PID 1 matter?

chapters.title: Dockerfile Essentials
points: A Dockerfile is a text recipe of instructions that BuildKit executes top to bottom to produce an image
FROM sets the base image, WORKDIR sets the directory, and COPY adds files from the build context
RUN executes at build time, while CMD and ENTRYPOINT define what runs at container start
CMD vs ENTRYPOINT: ENTRYPOINT is the fixed executable, CMD supplies default arguments that docker run can override
Exec form ["node","app.js"] runs without a shell and receives signals, whereas shell form wraps in /bin/sh -c
COPY vs ADD: prefer COPY, because ADD also extracts tarballs and fetches URLs, which is surprising behavior
ARG exists only at build time, while ENV persists into the running container
EXPOSE only documents a port and does not publish it, so -p is what publishes
USER switches to a non-root user, and HEALTHCHECK defines a liveness command
Example: FROM node:22-alpine, WORKDIR /app, COPY package*.json ./, RUN npm ci, COPY . ., CMD ["node","server.js"]
Mistake: using shell-form CMD so SIGTERM never reaches the app and shutdown hangs for 10s
Interview Point: CMD vs ENTRYPOINT? ARG vs ENV? Does EXPOSE publish a port?

chapters.title: Build Optimization and Caching
points: Layer cache: Docker reuses a layer if the instruction and its inputs are unchanged, and one miss invalidates every layer after it
Order instructions from least to most frequently changing: base, system deps, dependency manifests, install, source
Copy dependency manifests first (package.json, requirements.txt), install, then copy the source so installs stay cached
A .dockerignore (node_modules, .git, logs, .env) shrinks the build context and avoids needless cache busts
Multi-stage builds compile in a fat builder stage and COPY --from=builder only the artifacts into a slim runtime stage
Combine related RUN commands with && and clean up in the same layer (rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*)
BuildKit cache mounts: RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip keeps package caches between builds
Secret mounts: RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc keeps credentials out of image layers
docker buildx builds multi-platform images (amd64 and arm64) and supports remote cache export (--cache-to, --cache-from)
Example: a Go multi-stage build can shrink an image from ~1 GB to ~15 MB on scratch or distroless
Mistake: COPY . . before installing dependencies, which re-installs on every code edit
Interview Point: Why does instruction order matter? What does a multi-stage build buy you? How do you pass a secret at build time safely?

chapters.title: Volumes and Storage
points: The container's writable layer is ephemeral, so data written there is lost when the container is removed
Named volumes are managed by Docker under /var/lib/docker/volumes and are the preferred way to persist data
Bind mounts map a host path into the container, which suits development hot-reload but couples you to host layout
tmpfs mounts live in memory only and are never written to disk, which suits secrets and scratch data
Comparison: volume (Docker-managed, portable, driver support), bind (host path, full host access), tmpfs (RAM, non-persistent)
Mount syntax: -v name:/data (short) vs --mount type=volume,src=name,dst=/data (explicit, errors on typos)
A bind mount to a missing host path is auto-created by -v but errors with --mount
An empty named volume is seeded with the image's existing content at that path, while a bind mount hides it
Volume lifecycle: docker volume create, ls, inspect, rm, prune, and volumes outlive containers
Backup pattern: run a throwaway container that mounts the volume and tars it to a bind-mounted directory
Mistake: running docker system prune --volumes and deleting a database volume by accident
Interview Point: Volume vs bind mount? How does data persist across container recreation? When do you use tmpfs?

chapters.title: Docker Networking
points: Network drivers: bridge (default, single host), host, none, overlay (multi-host), macvlan
Default bridge docker0 gives containers IPs but no name-based DNS, whereas user-defined bridges add automatic DNS by container name
Host mode shares the host network stack, which removes NAT overhead but gives no port isolation
Publishing ports: -p 8080:80 maps host:container via iptables NAT rules, and -P publishes all EXPOSEd ports to random host ports
Containers on the same user-defined network reach each other by name and container port, with no publishing needed
Embedded DNS server at 127.0.0.11 resolves container and service names
Network isolation: containers on different user-defined networks cannot talk unless one is attached to both
Overlay networks use VXLAN to connect containers across Swarm nodes
Inspect with docker network ls, docker network inspect, and docker exec ... nslookup or curl
Example: docker network create app-net, then run db and api on it, and api connects to db:5432
Mistake: publishing a database port like -p 5432:5432 on a public host, which exposes it to the internet
Interview Point: Bridge vs host vs overlay? Why use a user-defined bridge? How does container-to-container DNS work?

chapters.title: Docker Compose
points: Compose defines a multi-container app in one compose.yaml with services, networks and volumes
docker compose up -d builds, creates and starts everything, and down stops and removes (add -v to drop volumes)
Compose creates a default project network, and services resolve each other by service name
depends_on controls start order, and with condition: service_healthy it waits for a healthcheck to pass
env_file and the environment key inject configuration, and ${VAR:-default} interpolates from .env
Named volumes are declared at top level and mounted per service, so data survives down without -v
Profiles let you mark optional services (debug tools, seeders) and start them with --profile
docker compose watch syncs or rebuilds on file change for a fast dev loop
Override files: compose.override.yaml is applied automatically, and -f compose.prod.yaml merges production settings
Example: web (build ., ports 8080:80), db (postgres:16, volume pgdata, healthcheck pg_isready)
Mistake: assuming depends_on alone waits for the database to be ready to accept connections
Interview Point: depends_on vs healthchecks? Compose vs Swarm vs Kubernetes? How do you manage dev vs prod configs?

chapters.title: Registries and Image Distribution
points: A registry stores and serves images, and an image name is registry/namespace/repo:tag
Docker Hub is the default registry, with rate limits for anonymous and free pulls
Private options: GitHub Container Registry, AWS ECR, Google Artifact Registry, Azure ACR, and a self-hosted registry:2
Workflow: docker login, docker tag app:1.0 registry.example.com/team/app:1.0, then docker push
docker pull downloads only the layers you do not already have, and each layer is checked by digest
Tagging strategy: immutable version tags (1.4.2), the git SHA for traceability, and a moving tag like stable only deliberately
Pin by digest (image@sha256:...) in production to guarantee the exact bytes
Multi-arch images use a manifest list that serves the right platform per client
Image signing with cosign or Docker Content Trust verifies who published the image
Cleanup: registries need retention and garbage-collection policies, since layers pile up
Mistake: pushing images with embedded secrets to a public repository
Interview Point: What is a manifest list? Why pin by digest? How do private registry credentials work in CI?

chapters.title: Container Security
points: Containers share the host kernel, so a kernel exploit or misconfiguration can lead to host compromise
Run as non-root with USER in the Dockerfile or --user, since root in a container maps to root on the host by default
User namespaces and rootless mode remap container root to an unprivileged host UID
Drop capabilities with --cap-drop ALL and add back only what is needed, because the default set is broader than most apps need
Never use --privileged, which disables most isolation and exposes host devices
Read-only root filesystem (--read-only) plus tmpfs for scratch blocks runtime tampering
--security-opt no-new-privileges blocks privilege escalation via setuid binaries
Default seccomp and AppArmor or SELinux profiles restrict syscalls and file access, and custom profiles tighten them further
Scan images for CVEs with Trivy, Grype or Docker Scout, and fail CI on critical findings
Smaller base images (distroless, alpine) mean less attack surface
Secrets: use Docker/Compose secrets or a secret manager, and never bake them into ENV or layers
Interview Point: Why is --privileged dangerous? How do you run containers rootless? Where should secrets live?

chapters.title: Debugging and Troubleshooting
points: First step: docker ps -a to see state and exit code, then docker logs --tail 100 -f <container>
Exit codes: 0 clean, 1 app error, 125-127 docker or command errors, 137 SIGKILL or OOM, 143 SIGTERM
docker inspect shows config, mounts, network settings, health status and the OOMKilled flag
docker exec -it <c> sh to get inside, and for shell-less images use a debug sidecar or docker debug
docker stats shows live CPU, memory and I/O per container, and docker top lists processes
docker events streams daemon activity such as die, oom and health_status
Crash loop: override the entrypoint (docker run --entrypoint sh -it image) to inspect the image directly
Port problems: the app must bind to 0.0.0.0, because 127.0.0.1 inside the container is unreachable from outside
Build failures: use docker build --progress=plain --no-cache to see full output and rule out stale cache
Disk full: docker system df shows usage, and docker system prune cleans stopped containers, dangling images and networks
Mistake: debugging only from the host when the issue is DNS or permissions inside the container's namespace
Interview Point: A container exits immediately, so how do you debug it? What does 137 mean? App runs but is unreachable, so what do you check?

chapters.title: Production and Orchestration
points: Production needs scheduling, scaling, self-healing, rolling updates and service discovery, which one-host Docker does not provide
Docker Swarm is built in (docker swarm init, docker service create) and is simple but has a smaller ecosystem
Kubernetes is the industry standard, with pods, deployments, services and ingress, and a steeper learning curve
Comparison: plain Docker/Compose (one host, simple), Swarm (small clusters), Kubernetes (large scale, rich ecosystem), managed (ECS, Cloud Run)
Healthchecks drive orchestration decisions such as restarts and routing traffic only to healthy instances
Set memory and CPU limits and requests for every container so one service cannot starve its neighbors
Logging: write to stdout/stderr, and pick a log driver (json-file with rotation, or fluentd/gelf) to ship logs centrally
Set --log-opt max-size and max-file, because unbounded json-file logs fill disks
Rolling updates and rollbacks: replace instances gradually and revert on failed health
Graceful shutdown: handle SIGTERM, drain connections, and set a stop grace period that matches your app
Pin image digests and keep containers stateless, with state in external volumes or managed databases
Interview Point: Why orchestrate at all? Swarm vs Kubernetes? How do you do zero-downtime deploys?

chapters.title: Interview Questions and Best Practices
points: Q: Container vs VM? A: containers share the host kernel and isolate with namespaces and cgroups, while VMs virtualize hardware with a full guest OS
Q: Image vs container? A: an image is an immutable template, and a container is a running instance with a writable layer
Q: How do you reduce image size? A: multi-stage builds, slim or distroless bases, .dockerignore, and cleanup in the same RUN layer
Q: How do containers persist data? A: named volumes, bind mounts, or external storage, never the writable layer
Q: How do containers talk to each other? A: a shared user-defined network with DNS by name
Q: COPY vs ADD, and CMD vs ENTRYPOINT? A: prefer COPY, and ENTRYPOINT is the fixed command while CMD supplies default arguments
Best practice: one process per container, stateless design, and configuration through environment variables
Best practice: pin versions and digests, scan images, run as non-root, and add a HEALTHCHECK
Best practice: keep images small and builds reproducible, and use CI to build once and promote the same image
Common mistakes recap: :latest tags, secrets in layers, running as root, no log rotation, and a missing .dockerignore
Interview Point: Walk through what happens on docker run. How would you harden and ship a production image? How do you debug a failing container?

chapters.title: Docker Cheatsheet
points: Containers: docker run -d --name n -p 8080:80 img, ps -a, stop, rm, logs -f, exec -it n sh
Images: docker build -t app:1.0 ., images, pull, push, tag, rmi, history, image inspect
Cleanup: docker system df, system prune, volume prune, image prune -a
Volumes: docker volume create/ls/inspect/rm, run with -v name:/data or --mount type=volume
Networks: docker network create/ls/inspect/connect, run with --network, and publish with -p host:ctr
Compose: docker compose up -d, down -v, ps, logs -f, exec, build, config
Dockerfile order: FROM, WORKDIR, COPY manifests, RUN install, COPY src, USER, HEALTHCHECK, CMD
Limits and safety flags: --memory, --cpus, --read-only, --cap-drop ALL, --user, --init, --restart
Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 app error, 137 SIGKILL or OOM, 143 SIGTERM
Registry flow: login, tag registry/ns/app:ver, push, pull by digest
